name: manual_bb17e2
claim: Methodology for "add durable protection against a class of bug" requests: a config file alone is not durable if nothing actually runs it. Concretely on orama-system's CIDF directory: the initial ask was framed as "add a tsconfig.json" to close a specific gap (a future TS consumer forgetting a default-value guard, silently producing wrong behavior since undefined comparisons evaluate to false with no exception). Adding the tsconfig and verifying `tsc --strict` catches the class of bug would have been a plausible-looking complete answer, but tracing the actual CI workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) revealed the deeper, real gap: CI never executed any TypeScript in this directory at all (no tsc, no jest, no npx -- only a one-line Python import smoke test), and pytest's testpaths never covered bin/orama-system/cidf/tests/, so a real, passing 37-test conformance suite had never once run in CI. The durable fix required three coupled things, not one: (1) the config file itself, (2) fixing whatever real issues the newly-strict check immediately surfaces on first run (config alone against untested code will surface genuine findings, not just noise -- confirmed directly: noUncheckedIndexedAccess found a real unprovable-non-empty-array case; mypy --strict found real untyped-dict and invalid-callable-annotation issues), (3) wiring the check into the actual CI job graph including its blocking dependency chain (a new job that isn't in any downstream job's `needs` list runs but never blocks anything, which defeats the entire purpose). General pattern: when asked to "add a safety config" for X, always trace whether X's classification/config is genuinely enforced end-to-end (present -> runs in CI -> blocks merge) before treating the fix as complete, not just whether the config file exists and passes when run manually.

decisions.notes: The single most generalizable insight from this whole exchange, applicable to any future 'add durable protection' request regardless of language or repo.
